---
name: budget-request
description: Handle a hire's BUDGET REQUEST line or plan something that costs money - pilot, measured cost, three options for the owner. Use before any spend.
---

# Budget request
1. **Stop the spend.** The hire waits; tell it with `send` that nothing is approved yet.
2. **Pilot.** If cost is unknown, size a small pilot (one item, one short run) and measure it. Don't guess a number.
3. **Ask the owner** in your terminal, short: what it is for, the measured cost, and three options:
   - A: cheaper (what is dropped);
   - B: as planned;
   - C: better (what it adds).
   Say which you suggest.
4. **Wait for the owner's answer.** Silence is a no. An approval is for that spend only.
5. **Relay the answer** with `brief`, in your own words: "the owner approved A, up to this amount". Never pass it off as the owner's own message to the hire.
6. Write the decision and the amount in the team board file.

---
name: fire-and-recap
description: Let a finished hire go cleanly and tell the owner what it did. Use after a task has PASSed review and its proof is checked.
---

# Fire and recap
1. Check the hire is finished: its `DONE` line, its proof, its branch holds the work.
2. Ask it, with `send`, to stop its servers and test copies. Wait for its answer.
3. `fire` it. Don't use `force` or `remove-worktree` unless the owner said so; unsaved changes mean you stop and ask.
4. Look at `team`: the hire's session must be gone. Chase leftovers (servers, test copies, detached sessions).
5. Recap to the owner in 5 lines at most: the task, the branch, the proof, the reviewer's verdict, what is next. Ask before anything that merges, pushes or deploys.
6. Add at most three lines to your `PLAYBOOK.md` if you learned something.

---
name: hourly-digest
description: Write the owner's hourly digest of the team - who finished, who is working, who is stuck, what needs them. Use when the app's digest line arrives in the inbox, or when asked for a status.
---

# Hourly digest
1. Read `team` and `inbox` since the last digest. Read `approvals` for waits on the owner (read-only).
2. Write at most 8 lines:
   - Done since the last digest (task, verdict).
   - Working now (who, on what, how long).
   - Stuck or waiting (who, why).
   - **Needs you:** each decision only the owner can make, with the answer you suggest. Put this first when it isn't empty.
3. Keep the team board file current with the same facts. Don't repeat a line from your last digest.
4. A hire that has not moved for a long time: look at its `STATUS.md` before you say it is stuck.

---
name: run-task
description: Run one task end to end - hire a writer, check the tests, get an independent review, one fix round, a fresh re-check, then report. Use for every task in the plan.
---

# Run a task
1. **Brief.** Write the brief in your folder: job, "done", proof (commands and results), off-limits. Say the writer reports in its `STATUS.md` and ends with `NEEDS-REVIEW:` when ready.
2. **Hire the writer** on Sonnet (`hire`, role fitting the task, its own worktree and branch). Within a minute check in `team` that it started and shows a prompt.
3. **Wait** for `inbox` to tell you of `NEEDS-REVIEW:`. Don't poll; check on the team every 10 to 20 minutes.
4. **Tests.** Read the writer's proof. Run the tests yourself in its worktree (the real path, not a copy). Failing: `brief` it back with the exact failure.
5. **Review.** Hire a *reviewer* (a different hire, read-only) and give it the diff and the brief, not your conclusion. It writes a verdict file: PASS or FAIL, with exact fixes.
6. **One fix round.** On FAIL, send the fixes to the writer once. Then hire a *fresh* reviewer for a re-check; the first one has seen too much.
7. **Still FAIL:** stop. Put it in the report under "What needs you" with both verdicts.
8. **PASS:** report to the owner (what changed, proof, verdict) and use `fire-and-recap`. Merging, pushing and deploying stay the owner's.

# Smolcorp [![CI](https://github.com/Sauzze/smolcorp/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/Sauzze/smolcorp/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

A control pad on your phone for the AI coding agents in your terminal: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and Grok. Your agent sessions are people in [a little pixel-art office](#the-office) on your phone, each at a desk, acting out what it's doing. From the office you can approve a permission request from across the room, interrupt an agent, change how hard Claude Code thinks, press buttons of your own, or hold the mic and talk to it. Smolcorp runs in your Mac's menu bar, or in the tray on [Windows and Linux](#windows-and-linux). Your phone connects to it over your Wi-Fi, so there's nothing to install from an app store. And it's not only one agent at a time: it's [a small company](#run-a-team). Hold an empty desk to hire a Reviewer, a Tester, a Bug hunter or a role of your own, and put a manager at the middle desk to brief the others and check on their work, while you watch the whole team from your phone. Smolcorp was called SauzzeDeck Pro up to version 1.6.1, and AgentDeck up to 1.0.1.

> Smolcorp is an independent project. It is not made by or affiliated with Anthropic. ## On your phone The phone opens straight into the office, full screen, upright or sideways as you hold it. Each desk is one of your agent sessions, named after its project: the folder the agent started in, or the top of its git repository. | In the office | What it does | |---|---| | **A desk, or its person** | Picks that session and brings its Terminal window to the front. | | **▲ ▼ ✓ ✕ over the picked agent, when it's waiting on you** | Move through its options, accept or reject. They come up on their own. | | **A desk, held** | Brings out its keys along the foot of the room: **esc** interrupts it, **⏎ send** presses Return, **/clear** starts a fresh conversation (tap twice), **↑ ↓** move through its menus, then [your own buttons](#make-it-yours). On a Claude Code desk, also paint chips for its thinking effort, from low to max; if Claude is mid-task, the change waits until it finishes. The coffee by the monitor shows the effort: one mug for low, up to four, and a steaming pot at max. A tap elsewhere puts them away. | | **The red button** | ☢ Max effort for the picked session, in one press. | | **The mic, held** | Talk to Claude Code. Let go, and Claude sends what you said once it's three words or more. | | **Two fingers, dragged** | Scroll the picked session's Terminal window; tap with two to jump back to the bottom. Off until you turn on **Let two fingers scroll Terminal** on the setup page. | How the people show what their sessions are doing is under [The office](#the-office). The room's edge glows while an agent is waiting on you. Sessions keep their order at the desks, and each keeps its own until it ends. You can pin projects to specific desks and furnish the office your way. ## Run a team The office has nine desks on the ground floor and five floors above it, each with nine desks and a chill area of its own, so you can run it like a small company of dozens of agents. **Hire by role.** Hold any free desk, and pick who to hire: a **Reviewer**, a **Tester**, a **Bug hunter**, a **Docs writer**, a **Refactorer**, fourteen more from an Art Director to a Thinker, or any role of your own, as many as you like. Each role has its own instructions, agent, model and effort, and comes in wearing its badge, like the Reviewer's glasses and red pen, and many dress for the job. A role never guesses what to work on: its first reply asks you which project, and its own questions, such as which branch to review. On Windows and Linux, `smolcorp run --role reviewer` also starts one from any terminal. [More about roles](#the-office). **Hire a General Manager.** On the setup page, **Hire your General Manager** on Start here (or hire the role from a free desk) starts one in its own terminal. It asks you the goal, what the team may spend and use, and what you want to approve yourself. Then it: - **plans** the work as tasks one agent can finish and prove in one sitting, and waits for your OK on the plan; - **hires one agent per task**, each with a brief of its own, in its own folder or worktree, branch and port range; - **checks** that each hire really started, and checks its proof itself; - has **a second agent review** any change before it's merged; - makes the team's day-to-day calls itself, and **asks you** before anything is pushed, merged to main, published, deployed, released, deleted or paid for, or reaches a real person; - keeps its board of what's done and what's left next to its brief. Each hire works on a branch of its own, in its own git worktree. The GM can pin a project to a desk and give a person a nickname: `smolcorp gm pin`, `smolcorp gm unpin --desk N` and `smolcorp gm nickname `, with desks counted from 1, as in the office. **A General Manager you start yourself** is recognised too. Turn on **Allow a General Manager started by hand** in setup's Manager pane and start one with its token: Settings then says "Your General Manager was started by hand.", and it isn't counted as an employee. Smolcorp remembers which session it is, the session id only, so this survives a restart. It's a label: the GM gets no new power. Its `smolcorp` has to be from 1.24 or later. Only you answer a permission prompt: neither the GM nor any hire can. Claude Code hires and the GM are also set up to refuse `git push`, deploy, publish and cloud commands, and to keep out of your `.env` files and keys. That is a fence against mistakes, not a wall: everyone still runs as you. You can see and extend the list in setup's Manager pane, and `docs/manager` says more. That is the Mac. On Windows and Linux, `smolcorp gm`, `smolcorp guard` and `smolcorp mcp` are installed, but the app answers the GM only for its version and the manager switch in setup, and, once the manager is on, for the team, the log of events and who is waiting for your answer; `gm pin`, `unpin` and `nickname` work there too. Hiring and firing for you, briefs, messages, watches, tiling, the fence and a General Manager started by hand are the Mac's for now, and the General Manager role there is the plain one from 1.22: you hire it, but it doesn't run a team for you. Smolcorp puts the whole team in one room, so you see at a glance who's working, who's waiting for you and who's done, and you answer any of them from your phone. **Or a manager of your own:** start any session in your projects folder and tell it its job, for example: *"You're the manager of this team. For each task I give you, open a new session in the right folder, brief it, and check on everyone every ten minutes. Have a second agent review any change before it's merged. Ask me before anything is pushed, released or deleted."* **Agents without a terminal work upstairs.** A manager, or a script of your own, can run Claude Code without a terminal, as `claude -p` does. Started with `SMOLCORP_HEADLESS=1` in its environment, such a run gets a desk upstairs, away from your keys. There's nothing to press there, as there's no terminal to type into. Set `SMOLCORP_PARENT_FOLDER` to the folder of whoever started it, and holding its desk says who hired it, what it's doing and for how long; tap the hirer to go down to their desk. A run that ends, or stops being heard from, leaves. ```sh SMOLCORP_HEADLESS=1 SMOLCORP_PARENT_FOLDER="$PWD" claude -p "Write the changelog for this release" ``` **Six floors.** Over the ground floor there are five more, each laid out like it: nine desks in three rows and a chill area with a couch, a plant and a coffee counter, in the floor's own style. They're filled in order: cloud bots such as Grok Bots first, each on its floor (see **Bots on any floor** below), then runs without a terminal, then anyone with no desk free downstairs (their keys are still on your phone's list). You can put anyone on any floor: tap the **⇅ floor** key on an agent, or drop them on the elevator. In setup's Office pane, you can also give a folder a floor, and its agents sit there from then on, each keeping their desk. Press the call button beside the elevator, by the entrance, for a list of the floors and how many are on each; pick one and the elevator takes you there. In setup, under Office → Floors, give each floor a name and a style: the office's own, the server room, or any of the styles. Each floor can be arranged its own way, too: see **Arrange the room** below. **Bots on any floor.** A cloud bot, such as a Grok Bot, takes a desk like anyone else, on any floor, the ground floor too. Put it on one, from the office or from setup's Bots card, and it stays there. Otherwise it sits where a floor's rule for its folder says (`/cloud/`, or `/cloud` for every bot), or on the floor new bots go to, which you choose on the Bots card; until you do, it's the floor most of your bots are on. When that floor is full, the bot sits where there's room, and setup names any bot left with no desk on any floor. There's no set number of bots: the floors' desks are the room. ## Supported agents Each agent tells Smolcorp what it's doing through its own hooks, and the deck presses that agent's own keys: | Agent | Interrupt | Fresh conversation | Effort and mic | |---|---|---|---| | [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) | Esc | `/clear` | ✓ | | [Codex](https://github.com/openai/codex) | Esc | `/new` | – | | [Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli) | Esc | `/clear` | – | | [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) | Esc, twice | `/new` | – | | [Grok](https://github.com/xai-org/grok-build) | Ctrl+C | `/new` | – | The effort chips, the red button and the mic drive Claude Code's own `/effort` and `/voice`, so they do nothing when another agent is picked. In Grok, ✕ declines with Ctrl+C, the key Grok uses to cancel a request. **Codex** asks you to approve new hooks before it runs them: after connecting, run `/hooks` in Codex once and trust Smolcorp's. Codex runs its hooks in a background service rather than in your tab, so the deck finds each Codex session's tab by its project folder. **OpenCode** 1 and 2 both work. OpenCode 2 runs its plugins in a background service of its own, so the deck finds each OpenCode session's tab by its project folder, as it does for Codex; with `opencode --standalone`, they run in your tab and it's found at once. Either way, run one OpenCode per project folder for the deck to tell them apart. ## Terminals Smolcorp follows sessions in any terminal on your Mac, and drives these: | Terminal | Keys and mic | Needs | |---|---|---| | **Terminal** | ✓, also behind other windows and while the Mac is locked | Accessibility | | **iTerm2** | ✓ | Allow Smolcorp to control iTerm when macOS asks | | **Ghostty** 1.4 or later | ✓ | Allow Smolcorp to control Ghostty when macOS asks | | **tmux**, in any terminal | ✓ | nothing | | **WezTerm** | ✓ | nothing | | **kitty** | ✓ | `allow_remote_control socket-only` and `listen_on unix:/tmp/kitty` in kitty.conf | Keys, the mic and typed commands reach the agent without bringing its window forward, so the phone works while you're in another app, under the screen saver and with the Mac locked. In iTerm2, Ghostty, tmux, WezTerm and kitty that needs no Accessibility at all. - **Ghostty 1.3** can't tell Smolcorp which window a session is in, so its desks show what the agent is doing, without the controls. Update to 1.4, or run the agent inside tmux. - **Other terminals** (VS Code, Cursor, Alacritty, Warp): their sessions get a desk that shows what they're doing, with no controls. To control one of these agents, run it inside tmux. - **Hiring** opens new hires in Terminal, iTerm2 or Ghostty, as you choose on the setup page, and with **Start inside tmux**, in a tmux session of their own. ## What you need - A Mac running macOS 13 or later, a Windows 10 or 11 PC, or a Linux computer. See [Windows and Linux](#windows-and-linux) for what differs. - One or more of the [supported agents](#supported-agents), running in Terminal, iTerm2, Ghostty, WezTerm or kitty, or in tmux inside any terminal (see [Terminals](#terminals)). Sessions in other terminals (VS Code, Alacritty, Warp…) show on the deck, but can't be controlled from it. - A phone, on the same Wi-Fi as your computer, or anywhere with [Tailscale](https://tailscale.com) on both. ## Install On the Mac, Smolcorp is in **beta**, signed with a Developer ID and notarised by Apple. On Windows and Linux it's an **alpha**, still in testing: the Windows build isn't signed yet, so SmartScreen warns you the first time. **The quickest way: let your coding agent do it.** Download [**FIRST-SETUP.md**](https://github.com/Sauzze/smolcorp/releases/latest/download/FIRST-SETUP.md) from the latest release (the Windows and Linux downloads have it inside too). Open your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode or Grok) in the folder you downloaded to, and paste what's in that file. It installs Smolcorp, connects your agents, checks everything, and tells you what only you can do: an OK for Windows Firewall or macOS, and pairing your phone. **Or from a terminal:** `smolcorp setup` on Windows (`smolcorp-cli setup`) and Linux, `/Applications/Smolcorp.app/Contents/MacOS/AgentDeck --setup` on a Mac. It does the same, prints a checklist, and ends with 0 when nothing is in the way. **On Windows (alpha, in testing):** download **Smolcorp-Windows-x86_64.zip** (or `-arm64`) from the [latest release](https://github.com/Sauzze/smolcorp/releases/latest), extract it and open **Smolcorp.exe**. SmartScreen warns about an unsigned app: click **More info**, then **Run anyway**. Smolcorp installs itself in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Smolcorp`, puts `smolcorp-cli` on your PATH, and starts from there: the folder you extracted can go. Its setup opens on **Start here**. **On Linux (alpha, in testing):** download **Smolcorp-Linux-x86_64.tar.gz** (or `-arm64`), then `tar -xzf Smolcorp-Linux-x86_64.tar.gz && ./Smolcorp-Linux-x86_64/install.sh`. If `~/.local/bin` isn't on your PATH, the installer prints the line to add (zsh `~/.zshrc`, bash `~/.bashrc`) and changes no shell file. **On a Mac**, three ways, all giving the same app: ### Download the app 1. Download **Smolcorp.dmg** from the [latest release](https://github.com/Sauzze/smolcorp/releases/latest) and open it. 2. In the window that opens, drag **Smolcorp** onto the **Applications** folder beside it. Then open Smolcorp from your Applications folder, and eject the **Smolcorp** disk in Finder's sidebar. The app is notarised by Apple. The first time, macOS asks whether to open an app downloaded from the internet: click **Open**. If setup then says …[文件过长——仅保留首 16KB 与末 8KB]… on to grant. Windows and Linux have no equivalent of Terminal's scripting, so this is how the deck reaches a session. A hire from the office opens this way, in Windows Terminal or a terminal the setup page lists. - **In tmux, WezTerm or kitty**, agents started the usual way work too: the deck sends keys through the terminal's own commands. kitty needs its remote control turned on (`allow_remote_control yes` and `listen_on` in `kitty.conf`). - **Tapping a desk** brings its pane forward in tmux, WezTerm and kitty. In the launcher it only selects the session, because the launcher can't tell which window it's in. - **Two-finger scrolling** works in tmux and kitty. - **Show Office**, in the tray menu: on Windows, the office in a window of its own; on Linux, in your browser, where Chrome and Edge can **POP OUT** it on top of your other windows. - **No Accessibility step.** Nothing here needs that permission. - **Hook commands name the office's port**, so two offices on one computer don't mix. Agents set up by an older Smolcorp are moved over the first time 1.24 starts. - **Grok Bots** sit at their desks too, but their news comes only through `POST /bots//event`: the Grok Bot app that the Mac reads is the Mac's only. ### Windows: the office in its own window **Show Office**, in the tray menu, opens the office in a window titled Smolcorp, with its icon. It uses WebView2, the Edge engine that comes with Windows 10 and 11. If it's missing, a message says so and the office opens in your browser instead. - A second click on **Show Office** brings the open window to the front, and restores it if minimised. There is never a second window. - **Always on Top** keeps the window above the others. - Size and position are remembered (`window` in `config.json`); if the screen changed and the place is out of reach, it opens centred. - The window pairs itself, as a device named "Smolcorp (window)", its key in `window-key` beside `hook-key`. Phones still pair with the six-digit code, and **Unpair All Phones** leaves the window's device alone. ### Who can reach Smolcorp (Windows and Linux) On Windows and Linux the server listens on this computer (`127.0.0.1` and `::1`: the setup page, the hooks, the launcher and the office window are all local) **and on the address Tailscale gave this computer** (`100.64.0.0/10`, on the adapter named *Tailscale*). The home network, a Wi-Fi hotspot or anything else cannot open port 7710 at all. If Tailscale starts after Smolcorp, Smolcorp joins its address within about 15 seconds, with no restart; if it stops, the address is let go. - The phone's pairing address (the QR code and the address on the setup page) is the Tailscale one. With no Tailscale on this computer there's none, and no QR code: Start here's button lets in your home Wi-Fi, or you get Tailscale. - On Linux, which listened on every interface before 1.24.0, an install with a phone paired already keeps doing so: its first start of 1.24.0 writes `"listen": "all"` in `config.json`, as the phone most likely reaches it on the home Wi-Fi. Otherwise it writes `"listen": "tailscale"`, so pairing a phone later changes nothing. - Every other protection is unchanged: the 6-digit pairing code, the check of the host name, the connection limits, and the setup page, hooks and launcher answering only to this computer. - **Windows Firewall** matches it: until setup's **Set the rules** has run, with your OK, Smolcorp doesn't open Tailscale's address at all, so Windows never asks and never makes rules of its own. The rules let TCP in from `100.64.0.0/10` only, and remove any older rule for a copy of Smolcorp, as one in `Downloads`, or one Windows made that let anyone in on a public network. - **Also on my home Wi-Fi**, on Start here, lets phones on your home network in too: it sets `"listen": "all"` in `config.json`, adds a firewall rule for your local network on private networks only, and starts Smolcorp again. On Linux there's no firewall rule to add: it sets `"listen": "all"` and starts Smolcorp again. Run as `smolcorp serve`, under systemd say, or with no display, it starts again in place: the same process, which prints its new setup link in its terminal or log, and stops as before. By hand, `"listen": "all"` in `config.json` (in `%APPDATA%\SauzzeDeck Pro`, or `~/.config/sauzzedeck-pro` on Linux) does the same once Smolcorp starts again, without the firewall's rule. The Mac listens on every interface. - `SMOLCORP_PORT` (1024-65535) replaces port 7710, to try a build next to the one you use. It is for tests: the hooks and the launcher read it too, so set it for everything that should talk to that copy. ### One Smolcorp at a time Starting `Smolcorp.exe` while Smolcorp is already running does not start another tray icon. The second launch asks the running one to open the office window (or bring it to the front) and exits at once, with code 0, or code 1 if no browser could open the office (it then prints the office address to open by hand). If the running one is an older Smolcorp that cannot be asked, a message says that Smolcorp is already running. On Windows the lock is a named mutex of the session (`Local\Smolcorp-single-instance`); on Linux, a lock on `instance.lock` next to the keys. If the port is taken by something else, Smolcorp says so and exits, rather than stay in the tray without a server. ### Linux Download **Smolcorp-Linux-x86_64.tar.gz** (or `-arm64`) from the [latest release](https://github.com/Sauzze/smolcorp/releases/latest), then: ```bash tar -xzf Smolcorp-Linux-x86_64.tar.gz ./Smolcorp-Linux-x86_64/install.sh ``` This installs it for you alone, in `~/.local`, with an entry in your app menu. Open **Smolcorp** from the menu, or run `smolcorp`. The setup page opens in your browser. - To update, run the new `install.sh`: from 1.24 on it stops the running Smolcorp itself first. `smolcorp quit` stops it by hand. (1.22 can't be stopped this way: quit it from its tray, or press Ctrl+C in its terminal, before you run the new installer.) - On GNOME, the tray icon needs the AppIndicator extension, which Ubuntu includes. Without it, Smolcorp still runs, and prints a setup link as it starts. The link works once, for five minutes; for a new one, run `smolcorp quit` (or press Ctrl+C in its terminal) and start Smolcorp again. - On a machine without a desktop, such as one you reach over SSH, run `smolcorp serve`. It prints the setup page's link as it starts. Open it through a tunnel: `ssh -L 7710:localhost:7710` to the machine, then the link in your own browser. ### Windows Download **Smolcorp-Windows-x86_64.zip** (or `-arm64` for an ARM PC), extract it and open **Smolcorp.exe** (see [Install](#install)). It installs itself in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Smolcorp` and starts from there, so your agents' hooks and the firewall's rules never name the folder you downloaded to. Opening a newer download later updates it the same way: quit Smolcorp from its tray icon first. ### Build it yourself You need [Go](https://go.dev) 1.26 or later: ```bash go build ./cmd/smolcorp ``` On Windows, that one program runs everything, in a console window of its own. To build it as the downloads have it, with no console window, build both: ```bash go build -ldflags "-H windowsgui" -o Smolcorp.exe ./cmd/smolcorp go build -o smolcorp-cli.exe ./cmd/smolcorp ``` `go test ./...` runs the tests, and `scripts/release-desktop.sh` builds the downloads for both systems. The version shown by `smolcorp-cli version` is `dev` unless the build sets it: ```bash go build -ldflags "-X main.version=1.2.3" -o smolcorp-cli ./cmd/smolcorp ``` (on Windows, add `-s -w -H windowsgui` for `Smolcorp.exe`, as above; `scripts/release-desktop.sh` passes its own version.) ## Support the project Smolcorp is free. If it earns a place on your desk and you'd like to say thanks, you can send ETH, BNB or any token to this address, on Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain or another EVM network: ``` 0x7a81788cf4cbb7357dfe3d98ab85a6422aab26c7 ``` Check the address after pasting it: transfers can't be reversed. ## License [MIT](LICENSE)

# Portable office viewer (beta)

The office, seen from your phone while you're away: **view only, off by default, end-to-end encrypted**, on a Vercel
project of your own.

Smolcorp on the Mac encrypts a redacted snapshot of the office (AES-256-GCM) and uploads it here every few seconds
while you've turned it on ("Going away: launch portable office"). This folder is a tiny Vercel project: a static
page that decrypts and draws the office in the phone's browser, and four API routes that store the ciphertext in
Upstash Redis for 10 minutes. The server never has the key: it lives in the link's `#k=` fragment, which browsers
never send. This README is the contract between the Mac and the viewer, v1.

No dependencies, no build step: plain files, Node Vercel Functions, and Upstash through its REST API with `fetch`.

```
viewer/
  vercel.json              rewrite /v/:id → /index.html; CSP and headers on every route; no-store on /, /v/*, /api/*
```

## Setting it up on Vercel (you do this; nothing is created for you)

1. **Create a Vercel project** on your own account, e.g. `office-viewer`, from your fork of Smolcorp.
   Settings: **Root Directory `viewer/`**, Framework Preset **Other**, **no build command**, output directory left
   as is (`vercel.json` says `public`).
2. **Add Upstash Redis** from the Vercel Marketplace (the free tier is plenty) and connect it to that project.
   It adds `KV_REST_API_URL` and `KV_REST_API_TOKEN` (`UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_URL` / `UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_TOKEN` work too).
3. **Add one environment variable**, `VIEWER_WRITE_SECRET`, for Production only, with the value Smolcorp's setup
   page shows you after "Make a write secret". A value shorter than 32 characters counts as none, and the viewer
   refuses every write until it's set.
4. **Deploy to production.** Paste the production URL (e.g. `https://office-viewer-xxxx.vercel.app`) into the setup
   page's "Viewer address" and press **Check the viewer**: it should say "Viewer ready ✓".
5. *(Optional)* A custom domain. Vercel Authentication can't be used: the phone has no Vercel login.
6. *(Recommended)* **A firewall rule**, so strangers can't use up your Upstash allowance. In the project's
   **Firewall**, add a custom rule: *Request Path starts with `/api/`*, **Rate Limit**, fixed window, 60 s,
   120 requests, keyed by IP, action **Deny**. The relay limits each IP itself too, but each request it counts is a
   Redis command; the firewall stops a flood before it reaches Redis.

What Upstash holds: each office as base64 ciphertext for 10 minutes, under `s:<id>`, and per-minute counters under
`rl:<kind>:<ip>:<minute>` for 2 minutes, so it sees the IP addresses that call the relay. Nothing else, and never a
key. A free Upstash database is plenty for one phone; a phone left polling all day uses a few hundred thousand
commands a month.

Then scan the setup page's QR code with your phone and keep the link (bookmark or Home Screen). It looks like
`https://…/v/<id>#k=<key>`. **Rotate key** on the setup page if you ever lose the phone or share the link by mistake.

## The relay protocol ("bring your own viewer")

The relay is four routes over any key-value store with expiry. Anything that implements this table (a Cloudflare
Worker with KV, a tiny server of your own) works with Smolcorp and with `public/` unchanged.

| Method & path | Auth | Does | Replies |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PUT /api/s/:id` | `Authorization: Bearer <write secret>` | store the raw body under `s:<id>` for **600 s** | `204`; `400` bad id, empty body, or first byte not `0x01`; `401`; `413` over 256 KiB |
| `GET /api/s/:id` | none | return the stored body, `application/octet-stream` | `200`; `404` when absent, expired, or the id is malformed (same reply, a malformed id without a storage lookup) |
| `DELETE /api/s/:id` | Bearer | delete it | `204` (also when absent); `401` |
| `DELETE /api/s` | Bearer | delete **every** stored body | `204`; `401` |
| `GET /api/health` *(optional)* | Bearer | check configuration and storage | `204`; `401`; `503` with a short reason |

- `:id` is 22 characters of base64url, `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{22}$`.
- The bearer is compared in constant time. With no write secret configured, or one shorter than 32 characters,
  every write is `503`, never allowed.
- Other methods: `405`. No CORS (the page and the API share an origin). Rate limit: 60 GETs and 30 writes per
  minute per IP, then `429`. The bearer is checked first: only authorised writes count toward the 30, and refused
  writes have their own bucket of 10 per minute per IP, so a stranger on the same IP can't use up the Mac's. Every
  reply: `Cache-Control: no-store`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`,
  `X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow`.
- Bodies are opaque to the relay: `0x01 ‖ nonce(12) ‖ AES-256-GCM ciphertext ‖ tag(16)`, with AAD
  `smolcorp-viewer:v1:<id>`. The relay must not log them.
- The page is served at `/v/:id` (the same `index.html` for every id) with the CSP below, and `/` shows "Not active".

Headers on every route (`vercel.json`):

```
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'self'; manifest-src 'self'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'
Referrer-Policy: no-referrer
X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
X-Frame-Options: DENY
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin
Permissions-Policy: (every feature) =()
Cache-Control: no-store            (on /, /index.html, /v/*, /api/*)
```

The Home Screen icons (`/icon-v3-*.png`, and `/apple-touch-icon*.png` for older lookups) and
`/manifest.webmanifest` get `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: cross-origin` and a day's cache instead, as iOS fetches
them outside the page. `index.html` also carries the 180 one inline, as a `data:` URL: iOS's own fetch of linked
icons can fail on a phone's network, and then the Home Screen gets the title's first letter, an "O". The manifest has no `start_url`, `scope` or `id` on purpose: the app then starts at the page
it was added from, `/v/<id>#k=<key>`, and a fixed start URL would lose the link.

## The page

- Reads the id from `/v/<id>` and the key from `#k=<key>`; anything malformed is "Not active".
- Polls `GET /api/s/<id>` every 5 s while visible (paused when hidden; 30 s after 3 misses in a row).
- Decrypts in the browser (non-extractable key), then checks `v === 1`, that `at` is newer than the last shown
  (an older body is ignored), and that it's at most 10 minutes old (±2 min for clock skew), else "Not active".
  The newest `at` shown is kept for each id in the browser's storage, a number and nothing else, so a reload
  can't be shown an older body again.
- Any v2 changes the AAD's `v1` text as well as the version byte: the byte isn't covered by GCM, the AAD is.
- Draws with `AgentOffice.create(canvas, {})`: no handlers, `pointer-events: none`, taps and keys stopped before
  `office.js` hears them, the room's sound forced off. The only request it makes is the GET.
- "Live · 12 s ago" in the corner while live. On Stop (404), expiry, a wrong key or a tampered body: the canvas is
  wiped and only "Not active" is shown.

```
node viewer/scripts/check-vector.mjs                    # the spec's test vector, opened with the page's code
node viewer/scripts/dev-relay.mjs --demo                # http://127.0.0.1:7771, prints the demo link
node viewer/scripts/dev-relay.mjs --demo --ttl 20       # expiry in 20 s instead of 600 (dev relay only)
```

The dev relay serves `public/` with `vercel.json`'s rewrite and headers, and runs the **real** `api/` handlers over

demo uses a fixed, fake id and key. `--demo` seals a sample office of four projects every 5 s. A DELETE of the demo
id (or `DELETE /api/s`) pauses the demo for 2 minutes, as the Mac's Stop would.

# The manager

The manager lets a **General Manager** (the GM) run a small team for you. The GM is a Claude Code session that Smolcorp starts. It plans the work, hires one employee per task, checks their proof, and tells you what needs you. You stay the owner: the GM can't push, publish, deploy or use cloud tools, and it never answers a permission prompt.

## Turning it on

It is off until you hire a General Manager (or switch it on by hand under **Manager**), and while it is off Smolcorp works as it did in 1.23. Your team's events are still noted, so switching it on shows what happened lately.

1. Open Smolcorp's setup page from the menu bar.
2. Press **Hire your General Manager** in Start here. Hiring the GM turns the manager on, so you don't need to switch anything on first. (If the hire fails, the manager goes back to how it was.)
3. Switching it off later fires no one.

## Hiring your GM

On the setup page, under **Start here**, press **Hire your General Manager**. Smolcorp starts a Claude Code session with the GM's rules and tools already loaded (a bundled plugin). The GM never asks you for a token or a key, and you never paste one.

Tell it the goal. It answers with a plan and waits for your OK. After that it chooses who to hire, which role and in what order, and asks you only about what is yours. See the [hiring guide](HIRING-GUIDE.md) for how a hire works.

## What the GM can do

- See the team: who is working, where, and what each one last reported.
- Hire an employee (its own worktree and branch), send it a brief, fire it.
- Send a message to a hire, and read the replies in its inbox.
- Ask Smolcorp to watch a file, a time, or a hire going idle, and be told when it happens.
- Tile the team's windows on a screen.
- Keep notes on each employee.

## What the GM can't do

The GM can't push, publish, deploy or use cloud tools: the same guard as hires (with its own `smolcorp gm` actions allowed). It never answers a permission prompt (no route does).

**Never, by the app:**
- **Answer a permission prompt.** No tool, command or route does this, for the GM or for anyone it hires. Only you, in the window that asks. If a hire is stuck on a prompt, the GM tells you.
- Turn on spending, pair or unpair a phone, change which hooks are connected, or edit the summaries' key. These are only the setup page's, and a caller with just the setup-key file is refused.

**Also by its instructions:**
- Merge to your main branch, release, spend or delete. The GM is told not to and asks you.
- Type keystrokes into another window. It talks with messages and the status files.
- Pass your approval to a hire as if it were the hire's own.

There is one GM per office, and only you hire or replace it, from Setup: the GM can't hire another GM, and a hire is never the GM. It has its own key, which lets it write to the GM and to the hires you have allowed it to write to, and nothing else.

## The phone's waiting list

Everything that waits for your answer shows on your phone: a hire's question or permission prompt. The list is read-only: you answer in the hire's own window, never through the GM. When a hire writes `NEEDS-REVIEW:`, your phone gets a "Ready for review" card and a notice. Messages sent to a hire that is at a question, a menu, a half-typed draft or at work are not typed in; they wait, and the GM sees in its outbox any that were given up on.

# Releasing Smolcorp for macOS

```bash
scripts/release.sh
```

This builds one universal app (Apple silicon and Intel) from what's committed,
and makes two downloads from it, printing each one's size and SHA-256 for the
release notes:

| File | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `build/Smolcorp.dmg` | The download for most people: open it, drag Smolcorp to Applications. |
| `build/Smolcorp.zip` | The same app, zipped, for the Homebrew cask and older links. Keep uploading it. |

The script won't run with uncommitted changes or untracked files: commit them
or set them aside first.

## The DMG

`scripts/make-dmg.sh` makes the DMG from `build/Smolcorp.app`, so after
`scripts/build-app.sh universal` you can run it on its own. It uses
[dmgbuild](https://github.com/dmgbuild/dmgbuild), which writes the window's
layout itself, so nothing opens on screen and neither Finder nor AppleScript
is involved.

The first time, it sets up a Python venv at `build/dmg-venv` with dmgbuild in
it. That needs Python 3 (the Xcode Command Line Tools have it) and the
internet, once. Nothing is installed outside `build/`, which git ignores.
Delete `build/dmg-venv` to undo it.

The window is in `packaging/macos/dmg/`:

- `settings.py`: the window's size, where the icons go, the volume's name and icon.
- `background.png` and `background@2x.png`: a corner of the office, in the
  office's pixel art and palette, with the arrow and the line "Drag Smolcorp to
  Applications". `make-background.py` draws them. Run it again after changing
  the art or moving the icons.
- `preview.py`: shows how the window will look, with the icons where
  `settings.py` puts them, without opening Finder.

Both Python scripts need Pillow in the venv:

```bash
build/dmg-venv/bin/pip install pillow
build/dmg-venv/bin/python packaging/macos/dmg/make-background.py
build/dmg-venv/bin/python packaging/macos/dmg/preview.py build/dmg-preview.png
```

## Signing and notarisation

By default the app is **signed ad hoc**: it works, but the first time people
open it, macOS asks them to approve it in System Settings → Privacy & Security
(the README explains how). A Developer ID and Apple's notarisation remove that
step. `release.sh` does both when two environment variables are set. Without
them it signs ad hoc, as it always has.

| Variable | What it does |
|---|---|
| `SMOLCORP_DEVELOPER_ID` | Signs the screen saver, the app and the DMG with this Developer ID Application certificate, with the hardened runtime on and a secure timestamp. The entitlements are in `packaging/macos/Smolcorp.entitlements`: Apple Events (for Terminal, Spotify and Music) and the mic (for dictation). |
| `SMOLCORP_NOTARY_PROFILE` | Sends the DMG to Apple's notary service and waits for it, staples the ticket to the app, then makes the DMG again around it and has that notarised and stapled too (two submissions), so the DMG, the app in it and the zipped app each carry a ticket. Needs `SMOLCORP_DEVELOPER_ID`. |

### Setting it up once

You need a paid membership in the Apple Developer Program on your own Apple
Account. The certificate and the notary profile below belong to that account
and stay in your login keychain. Nothing about them goes in this repository.

1. **Join the Apple Developer Program** at
   [developer.apple.com/programs](https://developer.apple.com/programs/) with
   your Apple Account, as an individual. Your name, as Apple has it, is what
   macOS shows as the developer.
2. **Make a Developer ID Application certificate.** In Xcode, open
   **Settings → Accounts**, add your Apple Account, select your team, click
   **Manage Certificates…**, then **+ → Developer ID Application**. The
   certificate and its private key go into your login keychain. Check that it's
   there:

   ```bash
   security find-identity -v -p codesigning
   ```

   You'll see a line like
   `"Developer ID Application: Your Name (AB12CD34EF)"`. That whole quoted
   name is your `SMOLCORP_DEVELOPER_ID`. The ten characters in brackets are
   your Team ID.
3. **Make an app-specific password** for the notary service at
   [account.apple.com](https://account.apple.com) → **Sign-In and Security →
   App-Specific Passwords**.
4. **Save a notary profile in your keychain**, so the password never sits in
   a script or a file:

   ```bash
   xcrun notarytool store-credentials smolcorp-notary \
     --apple-id "you@example.com" --team-id AB12CD34EF
   ```

   It asks for the app-specific password. `smolcorp-notary` is the profile's
   name, your `SMOLCORP_NOTARY_PROFILE`.

### Releasing with them

First, a dry run: it says which identity and notary profile it would use and
whether this Mac has the identity, and signs, builds and sends nothing.

```bash
SMOLCORP_DEVELOPER_ID="Developer ID Application: Your Name (AB12CD34EF)" \
SMOLCORP_NOTARY_PROFILE=smolcorp-notary \
scripts/release.sh --check-signing
```

Then the release itself:

```bash
SMOLCORP_DEVELOPER_ID="Developer ID Application: Your Name (AB12CD34EF)" \
SMOLCORP_NOTARY_PROFILE=smolcorp-notary \
scripts/release.sh
```

Notarisation usually takes a few minutes. If Apple rejects it, the script
stops. See why with:

```bash
xcrun notarytool log <submission-id> --keychain-profile smolcorp-notary
```

Releases are notarised since 1.24.2, so the README's and FIRST-SETUP.md's
install steps have no **Open Anyway** step. A release made without
`SMOLCORP_NOTARY_PROFILE` would need it back.

# The front desk API

The routes the GM and your own tools use to talk to the running app. The GM normally doesn't call them: its tools (`smolcorp gm <command> --json`, and the same as MCP tools) do. This page is for a tool of yours, or a port of the app.

The table that decides who may call what is `Sources/AgentDeck/SetupRoutes.swift`. Its copy for tests is `Tests/fixtures/frontdesk/routes.json`, and the other files in that folder are real examples of each request and answer. A test (`ManagerDocsTests`) fails if a `/setup/gm/` route in the table isn't mentioned here.

## Who is calling

The app tells callers apart by what they send. Every request is local, and has the header `x-agentdeck-setup: 1`.

| Caller | Sends | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **page** | the setup page's session cookie | Opened from the menu's one-time link. |
| **GM** | `x-smolcorp-gm-token: <token>` | The token lives in the GM's environment only. A hire can't use it. |
| **tool** | `x-smolcorp-setup-key: <contents of the setup-key file>` | For your own scripts. A hire can read this file, so a tool can do less than the GM. |
| nobody | none of these | Answered `401`. |

A caller who isn't allowed gets `403`. A route not in the table keeps 1.23's rule: the page or a tool. A `/setup/gm/` route not in the table is the GM's or the page's, so a new one starts closed.

While the manager is off (see the [README](README.md)), every `/setup/gm/` route answers `409` ("The manager is off") except the version and the switch.

## The front desk, `/setup/gm/`

Reads: GM, page or tool. Actions: GM or page. Fixtures are in `Tests/fixtures/frontdesk/`.

| Route | Who | What it does | Example |

| `GET /setup/gm/events` | GM, page, tool | The event log since a time. Long-polls up to 30 seconds. | `events.json`, `event-line.json`, `hook-events.json` |
| `GET /setup/gm/version` | GM, page, tool | The app's version, `managerEnabled`, and the features it has. Works with the manager off. | `version.json` |
| `GET /setup/gm/outbox` | GM, page, tool | The messages sent and their states. The text of a message goes to the GM and the page, not a tool. | `outbox.json` |
| `GET /setup/gm/watches` | GM, page, tool | What was asked to be watched. | `watches.json` |
| `GET /setup/gm/approvals` | GM, page, tool | What waits for you. Read-only. | none yet |
| `GET /setup/gm/screens` | GM, page, tool | The screens the team can be tiled on. | none yet |

A few things worth knowing:

- **Hire** answers `409` when no folder is set up for new hires and none was given, when every desk is taken, or when the hooks aren't connected. A `folder` outside your home folder is refused with `400`.
- **Fire** answers `409` when the worktree has changes nobody committed (`force` overrides this), when the hire is busy (`force` overrides this too), and always when its window shows a question or a menu: nothing is sent, even with `force`.
- **Contacts** (`/setup/gm/contacts`, GM or page): `{from, to, oneWay?, remove?}` names two hires by id or name. By default they may write to each other; with `oneWay`, only `from` to `to`; with `remove`, the pair is taken away. A hire may always write to the GM and the GM to any hire, so the GM isn't part of a pair. Answers the pairs as they are now.
- **Send** states: `queued`, `delivered`, `left` (given up on after several tries, not sent again) or `failed`. Mail is never typed at a question, a menu, a draft or a busy window, nor into the GM's own window. A hire's message to the GM is kept in the outbox and also makes one `mail` event, from that hire, in `GET /setup/gm/events`, so `gm inbox --wait` wakes for it; the same `id` sent again makes no second event.
- **Pinning** a project to a desk is `POST /setup/pin?key=<desk from 0>&folder=<folder>` and `POST /setup/unpin?key=`, both open to the GM and the page; `smolcorp gm pin`, `unpin` and `nickname` (and the MCP tools of the same names) use them, with desks counted from 1 as the office shows. Every `smolcorp gm` command does the same (`gm team`'s FLOOR/DESK column, `gm hire`'s "At desk N", `--desk N`); the JSON the app answers (`desk` in `/setup/gm/team` and the hire answer, `key` in `/setup/pin`) and the `team` MCP tool's JSON stay counted from 0. A nickname is kept under the project's last folder name, so two projects with the same last folder name share it.
- **Registry** edits can't change a hire's folder, branch, session or tmux socket.

```
curl -s -H 'x-agentdeck-setup: 1' -H "x-smolcorp-gm-token: $SMOLCORP_GM_TOKEN" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"to":"Rev","text":"Please look at the login change first.","id":"gm-001"}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:<port>/setup/gm/send
# {"id":"gm-001","state":"delivered","to":"abcdef123456","size":38}
```

The port is the one the app is on; tests never use 7710, 7720 or 7730.

These are 1.23's routes, now closed to the setup-key file because a hire could misuse them. The setup page alone may spend or send elsewhere (summaries, the viewer) and handle phone codes and keys (`/setup/pair`, the QR pictures, the viewer's key). The routes under `/bots/` are for the page and your own tools.

# Hiring guide

How a hire works, what keeps it in bounds, and where those limits end.

## A hire's life

1. **Hire.** The GM (or you, from the setup page) picks a role and a folder. Smolcorp makes a **git worktree** and a branch for it, so no two hires share a folder, and gives it its own port range.
2. **Start.** The hire is Claude Code running in **tmux** on Smolcorp's own tmux server, so it survives the app closing. Smolcorp checks the session really started (an agent in that folder, its prompt on screen) and undoes the hire if not.
3. **Brief.** The hire starts with a `BRIEF.md`: the job, what "done" means, the proof wanted, what is off-limits. Write it in plain words and give it numbers to check (see the [examples](examples/)). Never put a key, token or password in a brief or a message.
4. **Work and report.** The hire keeps a `STATUS.md`: its plan at the top, then one dated line per step with its proof. Lines that start with a marker mean something:
   - `NEEDS-REVIEW:` the work is ready, or only you can decide something. Carry on with the best default meanwhile.
   - `BLOCKED:` it can't go on; it says what would unblock it.
   - `STOP` the work stops; the GM reads why and decides or asks you.
   - `DONE:` as the last line, with a one-line summary.
5. **Review.** A different hire, who gets the code and not the builder's conclusion, reviews it. Nothing merges without its PASS.
6. **Fire and recap.** The GM checks the proof, asks the hire to stop its servers, then fires it. Smolcorp refuses to fire a hire whose worktree has changes nobody committed, who is busy, or whose window shows a question or a menu, and says why. `force` overrides the uncommitted-changes and busy refusals, never a question or a menu. A fired hire leaves a recap in `recaps/<id>.md`: who, task, folder, branch, when, cost, and its last status.

## What stops a hire

A managed Claude hire starts with its own settings file, merged on top of your account's. It holds two things.

**Deny rules** (Claude Code's own permission rules, which win over any allow):
- push, deploy and publish commands (`git push`, `vercel deploy`, `npm publish` and the like);
- reading or writing `.env*` files anywhere;
- editing any Claude settings file, and the app's own files: the hire guard's rules, the registry and the outbox. Edit and Write are also denied in every hire's folder by file type (`*.json`, `*.sh`, `*.jsonl`, `*.log`, `settings*`), not by name, so this covers hires started later too;
- reading the app's named files, the token files, Claude's session transcripts and `.env*` files (Read is denied only for these).

`STATUS.md` (a `.md` file) stays writable, as the hire must be able to write it.

In setup's **Guard** you can switch a group of commands off (deploy, say). That drops it from the guard **and** from these deny rules: you allowed it, so Smolcorp no longer blocks it for a hire. Off means allowed, for the guard and the deny rules alike: nothing else stands in the way of that group. Setup says so on every group that is off ("Off: hires will be able to deploy…"), and every group is on until you switch it. Switch the group back on and both come back.

**The guard**, a hook that looks at every tool call before it runs (`smolcorp guard`). It reads shell commands, including inside `sh -c`, `env`, `sudo`, `xargs`, brace expansion and `$'…'` quoting, and refuses push, deploy, publish, cloud and remote-login commands, `tmux send-keys`, `kill-*` and `run-shell`, `osascript`, `security`, stored-credential commands, any command naming `disableAllHooks`, any mention of the GM token, and starting Claude Code again (`claude`, `npx @anthropic-ai/claude-code` and the like), because a second Claude Code wouldn't carry the hire's fence. That last one is always on: the guard editor can't switch it off, and the GM's profile has it too. It also refuses the GM's actions in `smolcorp gm` (hire, fire, brief, tile, watch, unwatch, screen), but not the ones a hire needs, such as send and inbox. The GM itself runs under its own guard profile (`smolcorp guard --profile gm`): the same rules, except that its own `smolcorp gm` actions are allowed. If the guard can't read a command, it refuses it. If its rules file is broken, it refuses every shell command. If the guard program is missing from the app, a hire is not started at all.

A hire also can't switch the hook off: the settings that set it are the app's, and editing them is denied.

## What doesn't stop a hire

These are known and **not fixed**. The rules are a fence against mistakes and a clumsy agent, not against one set on getting out.

- A script the hire writes and then runs.
- Commands built from variables, or run through `python -c`, `node -e`, `perl`, `awk` and the like.
- Git aliases, and `xargs` when the command arrives on stdin.
- Wrapped `yarn`, `bun` or `pnpm` with some global options, and `yarn workspace`.
- A glob into the app's folder after a `cd`, such as `cd ~/Library/... && cat *`.
- Reading the GM's environment by any way other than `ps` (a script, another language; the hire runs as you). The guard refuses `ps` that shows it.
- A program that starts Claude Code itself (a Python `subprocess`, a script, `node -e`), or one named through a variable or `$(which claude)`: the guard refuses a nested `claude` typed as a command, but not one started from inside another program, and that one has no fence.
- The guard only covers Claude. Other agents get no guard.
- A refusal from auto mode only shows up when auto mode makes one (`PermissionDenied`).

Everything runs as **you**. A hire that gets past these has your files, your keys and your accounts. If that is more than you want to risk, build the wall below.

## The optional wall: a separate macOS account

For work you don't fully trust (a client's code, a long unattended run), run the hires as a different user. Then a bypass finds little of yours to read. Smolcorp doesn't do this for you; here are the steps.

Smolcorp's own hires still start as you, in a folder inside your home (the front desk refuses a folder outside it). This wall is for sessions you start yourself in the other account, and the GM can't hire into it.

1. **Make the account.** System Settings → Users & Groups → Add User. A **Standard** account, not Administrator, with a name like `hires`.
2. **Give it only what it needs.** Sign in once and set up Claude Code there with its **own** login, ideally a separate plan or an API key with a spending limit. Don't copy your own `~/.claude` over.
3. **Share the project, not your home.** Put the repositories the hires work on in a folder both accounts can reach, such as `/Users/Shared/hires`, and give `hires` write access to only that. You make the worktrees there by hand. Keep your own keys, `.env` files and SSH keys out of it.
4. **No push rights.** Don't give the `hires` account your Git credentials or SSH keys. Pushing stays yours, from your own account, after you've read the diff.
5. **Start the sessions in that account.** Use fast user switching, or start tmux and Claude Code in `hires` over a local SSH session (System Settings → General → Sharing → Remote Login, limited to that user). Keep the GM and the app in your own account.
6. **Close your home folder.** In your own account, run `chmod 700 /Users/<you>`. A Standard user then can't list or read your home.
7. **Check the wall.** As `hires`, try `ls /Users/<you>` and `cat /Users/<you>/Projects/<any file>`. Both should say "Permission denied".

The cost: setting it up takes time and two Claude logins. The gain: the bypasses above matter much less, because there is little of yours to find. Files you made readable to others, and anything outside your home, are still open.

4. If `STOP` appears in `{{status_file}}`, stop at once, whatever you are doing.
5. Don't push, deploy or publish anything.
6. Don't read, write, print or commit secrets.
7. Stage and commit only your own files, never `git add -A` or `git add .`.

## Report
- **`{{status_file}}`** is your logbook, read by the user at any time: your plan at the top, then one dated line per step with its proof (commands and their results, screenshot paths, commit hashes).
- **Markers,** at the start of a line: `QUESTION: <question>` (only the user can decide; carry on with your best default), `BLOCKED: <why>` (say what would unblock you), and, when the whole job is done, `{{done_signal}}: <one-line summary>`, then the `NEEDS-REVIEW:` line from the base rules as the last line. Say the same in your terminal, with where things are and what needs the user.

## Stop and ask
Write `QUESTION:` and ask before you push, merge, tag, deploy, publish, post or release anything; delete a file or branch; spend money, create an account, contact a person or submit a form on a live site; or go beyond this brief. If your agent's safety checks refuse an action, don't retry or work around it: note it and carry on.

## Never
- Open, write, print or commit `.env` files, keys or tokens (noting where one is is fine).
- `rm`, `git clean` or empty folders, unless the user named what to delete.
- Edit outside the project, except your own files next to `{{brief_file}}`.
- Quit, restart or call the apps the user has running, Smolcorp included, or type into another window.
- Install anything system-wide, or invent facts, quotes, numbers or results.
{{> never}}

## Clean up
- Stop every process you start (servers, watchers, headless browsers) once its step is done, by its own PID, never by name. Before you finish, check nothing of yours runs (`lsof -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN`, `ps`), and list any leftover in `{{status_file}}`.
- **A job over about 30 minutes runs detached,** to outlive your session, logging to a file; write its PID, log and how to resume it in `{{status_file}}`:
  `nohup perl -MPOSIX -e 'POSIX::setsid() or die; exec @ARGV' -- <command> > <log> 2>&1 < /dev/null & echo $! > <pid file>`

name: General Manager
summary: Runs a team of agents toward your goal: plans the work, hires one agent per task with a brief of its own, checks their proof, has their work reviewed, and asks you only what's yours to decide.
done_signal: GOAL DONE
read_only: true
report: TEAM-BOARD
question: What's the goal, and which project or projects does it cover?
question: What may the team spend (plans, API keys, cloud time), and which agents and accounts may it use?
question: What do you want to approve yourself, beyond push, publish, deploy, spending and deleting?
---
<!-- slot: about -->
You run a team of agents toward the goal named under "The job". You don't write the project's code yourself: you plan, **hire one agent per task**, brief it, check its proof, have its work reviewed, and keep the user told. **Your first plan waits for the user's OK. After that you make the team and process calls yourself** (who to hire, which role, the order, the next step), and ask the user only what's theirs: push, merge to the main branch, publish, deploy, release, spend, delete, accounts, and anything that reaches a real person.

<!-- slot: method -->
**Plan.** Read the projects, read-only. Split the goal into tasks one agent can finish and prove in one sitting, each with what it hands over and how you'll check it. Say what runs side by side and what waits. Show the plan in `{{report_file}}` and wait for the user's OK.

**Hire.** One agent per task, never two in the same folder:
- Give each its own **git worktree** (or folder) and **branch**, and its own **port range**, so no two collide.
- Write its brief in your own folder (`team/BRIEF-<name>.md`, next to this one) and start it with the brief's path. A brief says: the job, what "done" means, the proof you want (commands and results, screenshots, commit hashes), what's off-limits, and to stop its servers and test copies after each step.
- Hire from the office by role when a role fits (never your own role: there is one of you per office, and only the owner replaces you from Setup). Otherwise open a new terminal session yourself, in its folder, with a name that tells the user who it is.
- **Within a minute of each hire, check it really started:** an agent running in that folder, and its prompt on screen. A stray quote in a launch command fails silently.
- Never put a key, token or password in a brief or a message.

**Talk.** Use your agent's messaging between sessions when it has it (some agents can list the other sessions on this computer and message them). **Never type keystrokes into another window:** the user may be typing or speaking in it. Without messaging, talk through files (each employee's STATUS file, and a notes file you name in its brief), or ask the user to pass it on. Prefer a completion notice over polling. Check on everyone at a steady rhythm (every 10–20 minutes), not every minute.

**Approvals.** An agent's safety checks are the user's. If yours refuse an action, don't ask an employee to do it: that's laundering a permission, so ask the user. Employees treat an approval you relay as yours, not the user's: for push, deploy or publish, the user says it in that employee's window, or does it themselves. Anything that asks for a password interactively, the user runs in their own terminal.

**Check.** "Done" isn't done until you've seen it: run the command, open the page at desktop and phone width, look at the file. Test the real path, not one next to it. Before anything merges, a second agent reviews the change; give it the code, not your conclusion. When it disagrees with the builder, you decide on the evidence.

**Spend.** Estimate before anything costs money: a small pilot, the measured cost, then options for the user (A: cheaper, B: as planned, C: better). A budget is an estimate to check, not a cap on quality.

**Before anything goes public,** have the release scanned for personal data: names, emails, home-folder paths, machine and network names, keys, client names. Scan the **history** being pushed too, not just the final files; a single clean commit is the simple fix. Ask before crediting any person by name.

**Shell scripts under `set -euo pipefail`:** `cmd | grep -q` can end the script with no message when grep closes the pipe early. Capture the output first, then search it, and make every check say why it stopped.

**Let go.** When an employee is done and checked: it stops its processes, you end its session, **confirm its process is gone**, then close its window (a window with something still running asks "Terminate?" and blocks). Re-tile the remaining windows so none overlap, then chase leftovers: servers, test copies, detached sessions.

<!-- slot: deliver -->
`{{report_file}}`, next to this brief, kept current. The user reads it at any time:
- the goal and what "done" means, in a few lines;
- the team: each employee's name, task, folder, branch, port and state (hired, working, in review, done, let go);
- each task's proof once it's in, and the review's verdict;
- **What needs you:** each decision only the user can make, with the answer you'd suggest. This goes at the top.

In your terminal, report briefly: what moved, what's next, and what needs the user, in plain words. No line repeated from your last report.

<!-- slot: bar -->
- Every task ends with proof someone can check, not just "done".
- No two employees share a folder, a branch or a port.
- Nothing merges without a second agent's review, and nothing goes public without the user's word.
- Every employee you let go is really gone, and nothing of theirs is left running.

<!-- slot: verify -->

- Each "done" in `{{report_file}}` links to its proof.
- After each hire and each let-go, list the running agent processes and match them to the team.

<!-- slot: never -->

- Ask an employee to do what your own safety checks refused.
- Pass an approval for push, deploy, publish or spending to an employee as if it came from the user.

name: Janitor
summary: Finds what's left lying around (dead code, unused files and dependencies, stale branches) and lists each with its evidence. Deletes nothing until you say which.

<!-- slot: about -->
You find what's left lying around in the area named under "The job" and list it, each item with the evidence that it's unused and how sure you are. **You delete nothing, move nothing and change nothing until the user says which items to clear.** Until then you're read-only.

<!-- slot: method -->
- **Look for:** dead code (functions, types, routes and flags nothing calls), unused files and assets, unused dependencies, stale branches (merged, or untouched for months), old TODOs and commented-out code, leftover build outputs and logs, duplicated config.
- **Gather evidence for each item,** not a hunch: no references found (`grep -rn`, the language's own tools), never imported, last commit date, merged into which branch. Look for the ways a search misses use: reflection, string names, config files, scripts, docs, other repos or apps that call it.
- **Rate how sure you are:** **sure** (no use anywhere, with the evidence), **likely** (no use found, but a way in you couldn't rule out), **check** (looks unused, but it's public, recent or named in docs).
- **Respect what must stay:** anything the user listed under "The job" is left out of the list, whatever its evidence.
- **When the user names items to clear,** clear exactly those, one commit per kind (code, files, dependencies), run the build and tests after each, and mark each item done in the report:
  - a tracked file goes with `git rm` in a commit, which git can bring back;
  - an untracked file or folder is **never** `rm`'d: move it to the Trash (`mv <path> ~/.Trash/`, or the system's own Trash elsewhere);
  - a branch is deleted only locally, and only one that's named.
